text: A private recording goes online, and whether a schoolteacher keeps her job becomes something a room of parents intends to settle in person. Emi refuses to resign. That refusal is the engine: the argument has to be held rather than skipped, and the film gives it the time an argument actually takes. Comedy and drama are listed together and cannot be pulled apart here, since much of the cruelty arrives in a polite register, phrased as concern for children. What the case turns on is not the recording but the standing of the woman in it — who is permitted a private life and who is not. It took the Golden Bear, and European Film Awards followed for Radu Jude's direction and for his screenplay. A hundred and six minutes, and not one of them conciliatory.

Getting clean is the easy half; the second half is a long stretch of unremarkable days that has to be lived through without an audience. Clean is Canadian, made in English, and it opens where most recovery stories are winding down: a woman out of prison, her son in someone else's care, a life to be reassembled out of a job, a room and a telephone. Sobriety here is the condition of entry rather than the achievement — the boy is the point, and every ordinary afternoon gets scored against him. Olivier Assayas stays inside the part that other films cut, the months in which nothing decisive happens and everything remains at risk. Cannes gave its Best Actress to the lead, the Césars did the same and added the cinematography, which says where the weight sits: on a face in flat daylight, holding.

Tigers, lions and jaguars, painted by a man living among the poplars of the Po valley. Toni Ligabue built his menagerie inland and out of his head, and Giorgio Diritti gives two hours to the life behind it: a childhood at the margin, a self arrived at late and through paint. Screen biography tends to flatten into a list of achievements, and the counterweight here is plainly the performance — a European Film Award for the lead, a Silver Bear for the leading performance, David di Donatello prizes for film and direction on home ground. Harsh life and fairy tale at once: that pairing is the difficulty the film sets itself, since a story about being admired at last has to keep the poverty in frame. The valley is flat, wide and worked. The jungle is entirely interior.

The crime that put Madelon Claudet in prison was not hers; the ones that come after are. The order matters: a wrongful conviction arrives first and teaches her exactly what the law is worth, and only then does she turn to theft and to prostitution, with a single expense in view — an illegitimate son's medical training. Made in 1931, the film names that transaction plainly rather than veiling it. Seventy-five minutes is short for a life, so the compression puts the whole load on the lead, which is where the Academy's Best Actress went. Melodrama of this kind stands or falls on one question: whether the sacrifice is played as nobility or as a price. This one keeps the ledger visible. A woman is buying a future, and the currency is her own standing.

Charity as a logistics problem: how to feed people at scale in the seventeenth century, before there is an institution built for it. Monsieur Vincent takes the life of Vincent de Paul — priest, author, founder of two religious orders — and the interesting part of such a life is rarely the piety. It is the organizing. Saints on screen resist drama because the verdict is announced in advance, so what remains is friction: refusals, money, the distance between a vow and a full plate. Maurice Cloche gives it 111 minutes, time enough for the founding of anything to look like the work it is. The record is small and exact, an Academy Honorary Award and a Volpi Cup for the lead, and both point the same way: a film resting on one man's face while it argues for an unglamorous kind of competence.

Metello Salani means to get on in the world; his father went to jail, repeatedly, for the conviction that nobody should have to. The inheritance is the subject. A boy left more or less orphaned by anarchism grows into a man who wants wages and a marriage, and discovers that both are political whether or not he chooses them to be. Costume drama usually spends its budget on aristocrats; Mauro Bolognini's nineteenth century is scaffolding, rented rooms and the slow arithmetic of a trade. Love complicates that, marriage complicates it further, and neither can be separated from what a day of labor is worth. It took the David di Donatello for best film. What it risks is what every novel of formation risks: that a life will be mistaken for an argument. 107 minutes, period detail there to be worked in rather than admired.

The ship is built before any of the men are introduced, which settles early where the film's attention lies. HMS Torrin is a destroyer and also a workplace, and the account of her crew runs down through the ranks instead of circling the captain alone — E.V. Kinross drills his men toward loyalty to country, to him and, as the film insists, to themselves. It was shot in 1942 by people living inside the war they were describing, so hindsight was not available and none is attempted. That steadiness is hard to counterfeit. Best Picture and a screenplay Oscar, an honorary award, best film from the New York critics, a place among the BFI's hundred British films: a heavy record for what is, in method, a work chronicle. Noël Coward directed.

A shoe salesman picks up a hitchhiker and by nightfall has lost the car, the samples and the job. What follows is briefly revenge and then something else entirely: Paco puts Nino in hospital, and afterwards the two of them walk the same roads together, a Catalan and a Russian crossing a country that is home to neither. Manuel Poirier spends 124 minutes on this, which is long for a story with no destination, and the length is the argument — the film lives in the interval between arrivals, in the hours when two men with nowhere to be have to work out what they are to each other. Marinette, who stops for Paco after the theft, opens the other question, which is whether either of them intends to stay anywhere. Romance is among its genres, and the word fits, though not as a poster would use it.

A woman marries a physician she admires and does not love; soon after, she meets a poet who performs on stage. The Letter keeps her at a distance from him — the confession goes first to a friend who is a cloistered nun, then to the husband — so the drama is conducted almost entirely in speech, in rooms, with the decisive things withheld. Manoel de Oliveira sets two other worlds beside the marriage as quiet commentary: convent life, and Pedro Abrunhosa under stage lights. One has renounced desire deliberately, the other performs it nightly. 107 minutes, in French, made in 1999, with manners that belong to an older century transplanted into a present with no use for them. Restraint is not the style here. It is the plot.

The condemned man is never told the date; the guards arrive without warning, and that is the whole of the notice. The case the film makes rests on that piece of administration rather than on any softening of the four men waiting — André Cayatte, a lawyer before he made films, keeps their crimes in plain view and declines to claim that any of them is innocent. It is the harder position and the more durable one, since the objection to the guillotine does not then depend on who is standing under it. 117 minutes, made in 1952, at a length that lets waiting register as waiting. France's law enforcement establishment received it badly, and Cannes handed it a special jury prize the same year. The argument is procedural, delivered at the pace of the procedure.

Obedience is taught, like any other skill, and the film sits through the lessons. Sister Luke leaves a wealthy Belgian household for a convent, and Fred Zinnemann films the training that follows as a procedure worth watching in full: the rules, the corrections, the small daily surrenders meant to add up to a self set aside. The drama is interior and the film knows it, which is why the camera stays close and why a cinematography prize counts for more here than it usually would — the event is a face under a coif, deciding. Then war arrives, and a vow of obedience meets circumstances that have opinions of their own. 151 minutes, no raised voices, recognition at the Academy for the lead, the direction and the color photography. Nothing in it is argued loudly, which is precisely the difficulty being dramatized.

Karl Childers went into the state hospital at twelve and is judged, decades later, fit to leave. That is the setup entire, and Billy Bob Thornton — who wrote it, directed it and plays it — is in no hurry with any part of it: 135 minutes, mostly talk, taken at the speed of a man who assembles a sentence before letting it go. Patience is the method. The risk is obvious, since a performance built on impediment can slide toward imitation, and the counterweight is the writing, which gives Karl a moral logic that is consistent and entirely his own. The Academy recognized the screenplay and the lead. Released, he has to be put somewhere, among people, and what runs under every scene is the question of what is owed to a man others have reason to fear.

The deal is put like a contract: one seduction, carried out to specification, payable in a single night. Everything follows from that clause, and Stephen Frears films it as a workplace — two professionals in a shared trade, comparing method, keeping accounts, treating other people's marriages as raw material for a career. Costume pictures usually ask for the rooms to be admired; here the rooms and the clothes are equipment, which may be why the technical prizes it took were for costume and score. The eighteenth century is no refuge in this version. It is a system with rules everyone present has memorized, where the cruelty is legal, courteous and conducted in the third person. 119 minutes. The lead performance was recognized as well, and the pleasure and the problem are the same thing: the manners never break.

An Academy Award for sound went to a picture about a Senate campaign, which is a stranger fact than it first appears. Bill McKay is running in California with no chance of winning, and no chance is a form of freedom: he can say what he means, needle his own party, treat the apparatus as a joke he is inside of. What the film tracks is the price of that freedom as the numbers move. Michael Ritchie works in the register of coverage — crowds, handlers, overlapping talk, the candidate hearing his own sentences come back at him over a public address system — so the sound prize reads less like a technical footnote than like the method being named. Comedy and drama are both on the ticket, and no scene announces which it is. The screenplay, written from scratch, took its own award.
